name: Juvenile spring eruption
aliases: juvenile spring eruption of the ears

clinicalPearls: A benign photodermatosis, widely regarded as a localised variant of polymorphic light eruption, that chiefly affects the ears of boys and young men
It characteristically occurs in spring, often after cold, bright and sunny weather, and outbreaks may cluster among schoolchildren
Itchy papules and papulovesicles develop on the light-exposed helices of the ears and evolve into crusted lesions over a few days to weeks
The relatively unprotected ears of those with short hair are most susceptible, and a combination of ultraviolet exposure and cold is thought to contribute
The eruption is self-limiting and typically heals without scarring
Diagnosis is clinical, and the distribution on the ears in a young male during spring is highly characteristic
Management is with photoprotection of the ears, and the tendency often lessens with age
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile spring eruption is considered a topographical variant of polymorphic light eruption in which a delayed hypersensitivity response to an ultraviolet-induced cutaneous antigen is provoked on the exposed, thin skin of the helices. The predilection for the ears of boys reflects their relative lack of protection by hair, and the springtime clustering suggests that low ambient temperature acting together with ultraviolet exposure lowers the threshold for the reaction. As with polymorphic light eruption, the process is benign and self-limited.
additionalDifferentials: Polymorphic light eruption at other sites
Impetigo or other bacterial infection of the ear
Herpes simplex or other vesicular viral infection
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic springtime eruption on the ears of a young male
History correlating onset with cold, sunny weather and light exposure
Phototesting only in atypical or persistent cases
Skin biopsy reserved for diagnostic uncertainty
Porphyrin screen if erythropoietic protoporphyria is suspected
Bacterial or viral swabs if secondary infection or a vesicular infection is considered
redFlags: Marked burning or pain on sun exposure suggesting erythropoietic protoporphyria
Persistent, scarring or recurrent lesions outside the expected pattern
Features suggesting secondary bacterial infection requiring treatment
Extension to widespread or covered sites prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Juvenile spring eruption is benign and self-limiting, resolving over a few weeks without scarring; recurrences in spring are common during childhood and adolescence but the tendency usually diminishes with age, and photoprotection of the ears reduces further episodes.
pitfalls: Mistaking the crusted lesions for impetigo and treating with antibiotics alone
Overlooking the diagnosis because the eruption is confined to the ears rather than typical polymorphic light eruption sites
Failing to consider erythropoietic protoporphyria when there is prominent burning
Not advising ear photoprotection, so that predictable spring recurrences continue
references: British Photodermatology Group guidance on the idiopathic photodermatoses
management: Photoprotect the ears with hats, hair cover and broad-spectrum sunscreen to prevent recurrences
Apply topical corticosteroids to settle the itchy inflamed papulovesicular eruption on the helices
Relieve itch with emollients and oral antihistamines
Provide wound care with cool compresses for crusted lesions and treat any secondary bacterial infection
Reassure that the eruption is benign and self-limiting and heals without scarring
Advise that the springtime tendency diminishes with age, reserving phototesting for atypical or persistent cases
